unexplored is a bit of a mild name for how solid a roguelike adventure this game is

an even, uh, worse name would be
cave exploring cyclops

pros:
-vivid runs; where i have max stealth stuff and the shadows are providing genuinely safe harbour in hell-like depths, or ive gotten ahold of some extensive combo of materials ie copy scroll and scrolls
-a stack of maps for your adventure that are slow to explore and connected sparsely. you need to return after reaching the bottom. everything remains as you go up and down the y axis, stairs
-environmental hazards and chemistry. crafting/cooking of the try and fail variety. light sources and all its cons and pros. actors respond to distraction and alarms, like the alarm bell. religion, and conducts
-weird ass ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ orientation combat, where you effectively wield your hand equipment of choice directly, precisely in front of you, just like how doomguy hold his guns, dead center and w the sight near his chin
shields offer a very good barrier w the side they're literally on, in the live combat of swinging, stepping and strafing as you wait for cooldowns indicated by a differently shaded dagger
-distinct enemies. you will remember the ones that kill you and they will stress you out as you come up to them again even if its that pos mage goblin that uses all his randomly enchanted items and sundries as assigned by the universe run. or the spiders that jump. love spiders, normally, but the spiders in this are a legit minor threat
cons
-the waterlogged areas are AWESOME and they are also lethal run enders
-some iterations or runs can be bugged, in that old school procedural way. the religious system has a pray function which can get you a [necessary unavailable item] or whatever but itll happen. or itll appear to happen, but maybe you're just stupid/innattentive and haven't spotted the [necessary unavailable item]
-there are cryptic (but very thorough) mechanics normally found in hardcore rogues, namely; mystery. id-ing potions, scrolls and that shirt you just put on that now hurts and wont come off, is vital
-the crafting/stuff enchanting is a pain to really get to grips with (runes and enchant spots are sparce) as well as necessary. and not every enchant rock|enchant rock|weapon go together. 
crafting is fine it just contains set recipes tropes. you can make tea, which is hot (yes temp) water plus tea. you can also make strength potions (perm +stat) that are two bodyparts of midtier (at least) enemies.
-sudden, immediate, steep death might be far harsher than youd like, and the results screen might not give you much more context for whatever happened. dont let it happen again? dont lose your temper, the next run has a gun plus gun ammo ingredients almost certainly, or a new gargoyle enemy you've never hit with an unenchanted sword before, and couldnt possibly be completely immune to a tier of damage
or huge murmuring ogres patrolling thin paths across a void, ogres being capable of knockback
or a lich, which rarely isn't a challenge across tropes

Now that I've finally managed to beat the game on Hard level, after about 330 tries, I guess I can share my thoughts on it validly.

When I first took a look at Unexplored, coming upon it thanks to Unexplored 2, which is a very different game, I did not think that I was going to get much enjoyment out of it. After all, ARPGs are not really my thing. But the reviews were so positive, that I eventually decided to take a chance. And did the game ever grab me. From the simple, but not easy, fighting style, to the sheer variety of things in the game, to the clever interactions between certain aspects that it was a joy to discover, such as lighting a torch by dipping it into lava, the game is just fun to play.

The RNG is pretty excellent - I very seldom ran into unplayable situations, and even sometimes when it seems that you are stuck, there is a "pray" option that will resolve most blockages, although you will only have a few opportunities to use it per run without heavy penalties. But I rarely ever needed it, so that's no problem.

The single-eyed characters make the top down combat easy to understand. Sneaking is available, although it's been nerfed somewhat, but that is generally not a problem, except when you start as "The Fool". It is probably my only gripe with the game that the Fool doesn't start with a stealth +1 cloak.

Speaking of variety, you can play as 1 of at least 9 classes in the game, there are at least 16 different kinds of enemies, most of which have at least 1 type of boss version which serves as mini bosses, of which you'll only ever encounter 4 at most per run, there are at least 5 types of Dragons which serves as the end boss (except in rogue-likes it seems that the final boss is never the final boss, is it?), there are a variety of weapons (and magic) to use, lots of potions and scrolls, not all with positive effects, etc.

And all that is before you ever even get to the free DLC - none of which I have touched as yet. In short, if you enjoy a good rogue-like ARPG, I can heartily recommend Unexplored.

Below are listed selling points listed on the steam page, I will comment on them 

+ Fantastic Generated Dungeons (using brand new tech) + 

yes, unExplored is 8 years old by now and the procedurally generated dungeons are still quite impressive. My first couple of runs that made it around halfway into the dungeon I felt a sense of genuine magic. These kinds of games are always best when you dont yet know how far the rabbit hole goes.

on further replays i do feel the puzzles especially get a bit repetitive. Also the level generation can still cause some stupidness like a locked room and the only lever to open it is inside that same room with no other way to access it. Ive never seen this happen on the critical path though.

Still, usually the dungeon levels are good, sometimes fantastic. 

+ Real Emergent Gameplay with many Tactical Options +

Thisss is the best part of the game for sure. I guess you could say this about any game but unexplored is a game about problem solving and with all the interesting interactions between enemies, the environment, spells, potions and scrolls you have a good amount of tools for getting yourself out of a pickle. Throwing harmful potions into a swarm of enemies that have cornered you, casting disarm on an ogre and beating it to death with its own club, finding a corner to hide and perform a critical sneak attack on a boss that is chasing you. This is what its all about in my eyes.

+ Intense, Real-time, Dual Wielding Melee Combat +

the combat has a surprising amount of depth. it is also fun! Healing is scarce so your mistakes have consequences. you have to weigh the pros of cons of running into enemies or going for a risky swing. some enemies are immune to certain damage types and weapons have different attack speeds, ranges, swings and stats so you have a lot of reason to use different weapons and switch between them in combat instead of using the one sword with optimal stats or something

Stealth Mechanics (dungeon crawling like a real rogue…)

stealth mechanics are simple but cool. I dont think a full stealth build is feasible though... I wish daggers got an extra bonus on sneak attacks.

Over 50 dangerous bosses

The bosses are... okay? They are usually a slightly stronger enemy with a gimmick ability. 

Challenging, generated puzzles.

mmm, no. The puzzles are kind of ass. You find notes that say "go to a room and do a thing". You do the thing and if you did it right you get a reward. Thats it for the most part. I guess opening doors can kinda also be considered a puzzle because you have to weigh down pressure plates or drag a wind generator to a thingy but most of the puzzles in this game are only cool once.

Adaptive, original soundtrack

the music is okay

[h1]全体[/h1]
アクション制の伝統的ローグライクで、迷宮探索が楽しいゲーム(開発者はローグライトアクションRPGと称している)
ゲームシステムを調べる(探索する)のも楽しさの一部なゲームだと思うので、黒塗り多めにする
ダンジョン(地形,怪物,罠,謎,道具)と書物(謎解き等のヒント)が上手にランダム生成されていて、毎回、新鮮な迷宮で遊べる
アクション要素と伝統的ローグライク要素が3:7ぐらいで配合。アクションにそこまで疾走感や派手さがあるわけではなく、硬派に迷宮を攻略するゲーム

[h1]ダンジョン[/h1]
・Cyclic Dungeon Generationという技術でランダム生成された迷宮が本当に本当に面白い。「この部屋は前も見た、またあれするんでしょ？」という展開が少ない。このゲームを体験した後だと、他のローグライクのランダム生成迷宮が手抜きなんじゃないかと思うぐらいよくできている
・怪物の種類は沢山。ダンジョンのボスは[spoiler]ドラゴン系[/spoiler]だが、中ボスや怪物は毎回知らないのと出会うぐらい種類が多い
・怪物や毒ガス出てくる罠や無敵のタレットが待ち構えている[spoiler]だけでなく、部屋に半永久的に閉じ込めてきたり、下の階層へ突き飛ばされたり、橋が崩れたりといった危険な状況に直面することもある。逆に言うと、敵を同じ目に合わせることも可能[/spoiler]
・探索に役に立つ情報が書かれた本を拾って読む

[h1]アクション[/h1]
・一見すると似ている武器が多いが、攻撃範囲,タメ時間,ダメージ量,ダメージ種などが違う
・人型の怪物は自分が使うこともできる装備を使い、仕様が共通している
・[spoiler]不意打ちすると大ダメージが入る。卑怯なと思うかもしれないが、大人数の怪物、罠がしかけてある敵地、透明化する敵が待ち構えているので、やらなきゃやられる[/spoiler]
・武器を振った後のクールタイムに入るなどするとスローモーションになるオプションがある。アクションが苦手な人やアクションよりもターン制を遊びたい人に対する配慮だと思う。アクションに疾走感が欲しいならOFFにした方がいい

[h1]ローグライク[/h1]
・耐性持ちの敵がいるので、武器等を使い分けたり工夫する必要がある
・杖,ポーション,一部の装備は効果が不明で判別していく必要がある(伝統的ローグライクでよくあるシステム)。昨今のゲームでは廃れた要素なので人を選ぶかもしれない。呪われた装備は外せないので、場合によっては大変な目に遭う
・道具を組み合わせる"調合",供え物と道具等を交換する"祭壇",装備と素材を合体させる"鍛造",詰まった時の"祈り"という要素がある。これらの要素もそうだが基本的にどの要素も、落ちている本から部分的に情報収集して後は手探り。この辺りの伝統的ローグライクのやり方は人を選ぶかもしれない。easyモードであればこれらをそこまで上手に使いこなせなくてもクリアできるので、やりながらゆっくり覚えればいい
・死んだ時の所持金や持ち帰った金品を使って、1回限りの装備や道具が買える。気楽に無料装備で稼ぐ、ガチガチに準備をして生還を目指すといったプレイスタイルを好きに選べるし、難易度を調整できる。ゲームが難しいと思ったら、とりあえず回復をたくさん持ち込めばいい
・レベル上げ要素はほぼない。実績を達成することで職業(最初の初期状態)が開放されたり、店の品揃えが良くなる
・元祖ローグと同じように、ダンジョンから帰ってくるまでがゴール。一度通った道を帰るわけだが、スルーした敵が残っていたり、新たな脅威と向き合う必要がある

[h1]その他[/h1]
・お値段の割にたくさん遊べる。50時間ほどプレイしたが、まだまだ知らない敵,解けない謎,クリアできない難易度がある
・異なるモードが追加される、無料DLCが3つもある
・日本語非対応。日記のような探索メモを読むので、それなりの英語力かツールが必要
・いい音楽

[h1]不満点[/h1]
・読んだ本の情報を再閲覧することはできるが整理する方法はゲーム内でほぼ用意されていない。例えば、拾った調合レシピを元にこちらでメモするなり暗記することが必要。何階で入手した情報か忘れてしまう
・謎解きのヒントを見つけることができるが、どの部屋のことか分からない。試行回数は有限なので解けないことも多い。単に自分の実力や英語能力の不足かもしれないが…
・少しでも謎解きの成功率を上げるために色んな階層を行ったり来たりする時はあまり面白くない
・多少異なる初期状態でゲームを開始できるが、大体やることは似ている
・見つけるメモに書かれた内容がダンジョンに反映されていないことがたまにある
・ゲームを中断して時間が空くと謎解きや迷宮のヒントの記憶が薄れて、ゲーム内のメモを参照して補完する必要があるが面倒になって一からやり直しすることになる

Some good things I noted during play

+ The game really starts to open up and show you how much there is the more you play. It doesn't show you a menu that says 2/50 unlocked like a lot of other games. You go into a run, complete achievements, and earn new things to use on your next run. This may be additional items you can purchase at the start of your run or different loadouts to use. It's not much but the surprise factor was nice.

+ The character design is charming all around. The look and sounds of your main character are absolutely adorable. The little notes you can find in the game giving you some hints about the Boss you will face are nice as well. I LOVE Unexplored! My only wish was that Devs might add a little bit more secret sauce to the endgame content. The fact that weapons can basically only be enchanted one type to +5 for example felt like such a limiting thing, as did the extremely spartan gear slots and attributes. I get that they were aiming for fewer itemization choices with greater individual impact and a generally greater focus on actually playing the game and interacting with mechanics rather than wasting time stuck in menus or pondering gear or build choices, but I still just feel like the late game content was too lacking in diversity or interest for this to ever be considered up there with one of the truly greats of this genre. 

As it stands, despite the fact I can't honestly quite say that I think Unexplored is an all time great, but I still highly recommend it, and it's one of my favourites in years just for its conceptual creativity and masterful execution. Unexplored is the only title I have ever encountered that is real time yet still feels genuinely worthy of association with the roguelike descriptor. Every other so-called "action roguelike" or "real time roguelike" I have encountered has played like some sort of top-down action game or twin stick shooter and we already have the term "roguelite" to describe such games. 

Gungeon, Isaac, and so on are all excellent titles while in their element and I respect their developers (although some of the latter slop clones not so much), but nevertheless I want their style of content kept clearly separate conceptually from the bona fide roguelike, because they really are two quite different styles. Unexplored, however, is a title I make an exception for, because it's one title that isn't just an action game that borrowed a few elements from the roguelike genre, it's genuinely a true roguelike experience at its core, just made real time, and there's a world of difference between an action game with roguelike elements and a roguelike with real time gameplay.

So why do I say that this has genuine roguelike DNA while others just have "elements". It all comes down to the fundamentals of how the game "feels" to play. Unexplored achieves those nail-biting will I die / won't I die moments, the true RNG madness where you both die and win the world for no truly fair reason, and of course that wonderful series of moments rushing to the finish / surface / ending with the object of Yendor in hand, Indiana Jones style dungeon cave in happening rapidly behind you. These core roguelike experience qualities were all part of Unexplored and done so very well to boot, and this recreation of the core genre charm and zany randomness and unique moments all make Unexplored a bona fide roguelike experience in a way that Gungeon or Isaac or many similar titles are not.

My only wish is that they made the end game content just before the final escape a little bit richer, got the basics done right with a little more reliability, and put the effort in to make a denser pool of content with the philosophy that "players shouldn't be seeing the same thing twice until they've played several runs". Instead, there are all the hallmarks of things being rushed out just a little bit too quickly, there is that all too common indication that somewhere along the line, passion project turned into "let's just get this thing shipped", presumably because their team was just that little bit too small to really get the game done exactly as it was crying out to be completed. 

I believe this game could have gone down in history as one of the best games of all time "to those in the know" (same way as any trad rogue like) had they done this, but because they did not, I think that all told Unexplored exists in a twilight zone just between a valiant development effort that tried hard but didn't quite pull things off and genuine greatness. I don't really feel right describing it as sitting comfortably in either of these two camps, it straddles both, achieving the feeling of one in some moments, and the other in different moments.

When it comes to this greatness-fail paradox, let's talk examples. The dungeon contains riddles and puzzles and secrets that are just wonderful. They feel so very much fun to discover and work out, and you're always excited to win some extra loot because roguelike scarcity has been done just right, *chefs kiss* levels of scarcity perfection. But then you've discovered all of these little nuggets of game play fun by type before long, perhaps even just a few floors in... If ONLY they'd simply made a few more different "types" of them! If ONLY the Devs had implemented just a few more novel non-combat interactions, a few more magic enchanting types, a few more weapon options, a few more enemy types, a few more secrets and most of all just a few more dungeon puzzles, it would have reached a different level.

This is where the most disappointing part of this story must be said. Given the reality that I LOVED this game but saw it as just being a few hundred more hours of pain and passion away from true greatness and the opportunity to claim a spot in gaming history alongside ToME or ADoM, I had hoped that Unexplored 2 would remedy the content shortcomings and bumpy pacing of Unexplored 1 and produce that final work of art that Unexplored was always crying out to be. Instead, they took Unexplored 2 in a completely different direction and I can't pretend it was anything other than a huge letdown for me. I hope that one day I might get the chance to play some sort of Unexplored 1 - Part 2 made by either the original devs or some skilled modders who can finally bring this title to the final form that my head always dreamed that it could be, but until that time, it's still definitely a title that's worth picking up and playing.

If you have less than 10 hours in this I find it hard to believe you actually engaged with the game on its level. This a hard roguelike with a lot going for it - the generation is well put together and levels typically flow nicely. There are enough unique artifacts/enemies/bosses/rooms that I'm still finding new stuff with 2-3 dozen runs under my belt. There may be a few mechanics you are unaware of at first which you *need* to know about in order to progress, but you also have the option if you are genuinely stuck at praying near a door for it to open. The game has a pause system that you *should* be using when things hit the fan (this is very similar to people complaining about unfairness in FTL when there is almost always a way out of a problem). Everything is a puzzle- how do I fight this enemy, what are they weak to, *should* I fight this enemy? In terms of game knowledge to be successful, there is a lot you will need to pick up and some things you might not learn in 100-300 hours of playtime- the way I enjoyed and would tepidly recommend is go in blind, get a dozen or so good runs under your belt, and look up some things if you feel like you are grinding your wheels or a winning run would be dashed because you didn't know something ( I did this when I didn't want to lose a run not knowing the 50+ ways you can enchant gear for wildly different results, for example). Like most roguelikes, there are some levels that are just nasty or scenarios that are rather unfair (entering a new floor and immediately getting pelted with a potion, for example). Every death I've had however has been a learning experience in realizing choices I could have made to survive, damage is *usually* fairly low and you can almost always back out of engagements or reassess your approach.

The progression system is also fun, achievements are tied directly into more supplies and unlocking characters and I look forward to playing more on hard to permanently improve their loadouts. The most major criticism I have for this game is you are incentivized to backtrack A LOT to get the most out of the floors, and if you have a low tolerance for this it's a good reason to avoid the game. It's the sort of game I enjoy playing with some other media to watch on the boring bits.

Unexplored is an action roguelike, as it says on the tin. It has a lot of options for players provided you're willing to put in the work to unlock the options. ~20 hours into the game and I've yet to unlock all of them, not by virtue of how many there are but how rare some of the requirements are. In my time I've seen less than 10 orcs, which drop items necessary to unlock the Berserker. I've never had a firearm and just got my first crossbow in the last hour or so of playing.
The game holds a wide variety of weapons and armor, most of which are interchangeable without actually affecting play. The difference between a Sword, a Longsword, and a Greatsword isn't damage but a slight increase of range. Armors are more limited but there's enough names and sprites to make them feel distinct.
The dungeon itself is complex in its generation and puzzles, borderline arcane at times. Solutions to puzzles can spawn on floors above or below it and they frequently do, which wouldn't be such an issue if the game didn't crash when you go to a floor you've already been to. Some dungeon seeds are unplayable because of how many high-skill enemies spawn in the first 3 floors. Some dungeon seeds are unplayable because a floor spawns without any staircases or they're locked behind doors without a way to open them apart from praying to the Gods.
On that note, the prayer system is interesting. It serves as an occasional "Get out of jail free" card, also sometimes a "I hope you like your run ending with 30 bats spawning in this cramped corridor right on top of you" card. From what I can tell there are three variations to prayers being answered. the White answers are the most basic and can temporarily open doors, give hints, teleport you randomly on the same floor, and unlock chests. The Gold Answer permanently opens things, and the Red Answer does all of the above with the caveat that enemies will spawn after you go through.
The mechanics are incredibly deep, there's a system for enchanting, brewing, and making scrolls that I rarely get the chance to use because the materials are hard to come by. Though deep, they're also relatively unpolished. Moving between floors you've visited can cause game-breaking lag or the game to crash altogether, restarting a dungeon on the same seed(from the death menu) starts you on the same floor on which you died, unfair enemies can put you in a situation where literally all of your weapons have been knocked down a floor and into lava. It's particularly annoying when your arrows decide to veer off-course halfway through their flight path. Even on the lowest difficulty setting it's not hard to find yourself with heavily damaged gear because a single corrosive enemy spawned in the first room of the floor you're going into and the loading screen took its sweet time. Should all else fail, I've had saves corrupt and become unplayable while traveling between floors.

Make no mistake, I love Unexplored. It's one of a kind. I haven't found anything quite like it. Its art style is fantastic, the enemy variety is creative, the achievements, classes, and other rewards are cool. Dare I say it, cooler than any other roguelike's system. It could use a nice polishing, something to iron out the issues and make things less frustrating. The highs are incredibly high and the lowest lows might see you wanting to remove the game from your library.

[i][b]Vous voilà face au donjon de la damnation, l'immense complexe souterrain qui renferme le plus puissant artefact de la création, l'amulette de Yendor. Armé de votre dague, de votre ingéniosité et surtout de prudence, vous passez la porte.[/b][/i]

Unexplored s'inspire fortement du Roguelike et les amateurs du genre retrouveront un côté Nethack. Si vous ne connaissez pas le genre, aucun problème, le Roguelike est un genre fortement complexe et chronophage qui n'est clairement pas pour tout le monde. Unexplored innove sur plus d'un point et propose surtout un gameplay dynamique et aisé d'accès qui parvient à distiller sous une forme plus digeste quelques-unes des richesses du genre.

 [h1]The binding of Rodney[/h1]

Vous incarnez le personnage au centre de l'écran, les déplacements sont faits avec les touches directionnelles et la souris est utilisée pour se tourner (un système de contrôle qui s'adapte très bien aux manettes). Vous utiliserez la plupart du temps une arme de mêlée : lorsque celle-ci entre en contact avec un ennemi, il subit des blessures. Bien entendu, si votre adversaire possède lui aussi un truc pointu en main, il pourra vous toucher de la même manière. A chaque fois qu'une arme touche un ennemi ou une autre arme, elle se "décharge" et devient inutile l'espace de quelques secondes, ce qui vous permettra notamment de parer avec votre arme.

 [h1]Se battre avec la tige[/h1]

Si le système de combat est plutôt intuitif et peut simplement se résumer à "toucher l'adversaire avec une extrémité pointue", il est souvent très difficile à contrôler. Si votre adversaire possède une arme plus longue que la vôtre par exemple, il sera très difficile de pénétrer sa défense pour lui porter un coup. S'il possède un bouclier et vous une arme à deux mains, il pourra aisément bloquer vos coups et vous laisser sans défense. De plus, vos ennemis seront rarement seuls et vous contraindront à vous tourner en tout sens pour ne pas être débordé. Dans l'ensemble, il sera difficile de ne pas passer votre temps à subir des dégâts, et en cas de mort, c'est retour à la case départ.

 [h1]Temps mort ![/h1]

Si le système de combat est si difficile à maîtriser, ce n'est pas par mauvais design mais par choix. S'engager dans un combat doit être une décision que vous pèserez lourdement, découvrir un nouvel ennemi doit être une expérience stressante qui vous poussera à réfléchir à la meilleure manière d'aborder le problème.
Les blessures peuvent être guéries en mangeant des rations ou avec une potion de soin, mais ces dernières sont malheureusement très rares et si les rations sont bien plus fréquentes, elles prennent du temps à être employer et ne pourrons pas vous sauver la vie si des adversaires imprévus vous coincent dans un coin du donjon.

 [h1]Un petit coup et ça repart[/h1]

Pour vous sortir des situations les plus épineuses, il vous faudra employer vos ressources intelligemment. Pas question de juste gagner un peu d'expérience pour revenir plus tard, il n'y a pas de niveau et s'il existe une progression de l'équipement, son impact n'est pas si majeur que cela, donc à défaut de pouvoir faire appel à la force brute, il faudra être ingénieux et employer des consommables.
Vous trouverez tout un tas de consommables au cours de votre exploration : potions, baguettes, flèches et autres choses qui peuvent vous permettre de vous sortir de n'importe quelle situation avec un peu de débrouillardise. Avec suffisamment de flèches, tuer un troll à travers un fossé devient trivial. Avec une baguette de boule de feu, une chauve-souris géante sera vite transformée en casse-croûte.

 [h1]Expérience, cruelle maîtresse[/h1]

Employer trop peu de consommables et vous mourrez avec un inventaire plein d'objets qui auraient pu vous sauver. Employez-en n'importe comment et vous finirez désarmé dans des situations critiques. Qui plus est, transformer une baguette de nuage toxique en arme mortelle demande parfois un peu d'imagination.
L'autre problème, c'est que la plupart des objets trouvés dans le donjon ne sont pas identifiées à la base, il vous faudra employer les parchemins une première fois pour découvrir le sort inscrit dessus, boire les potions en espérant qu'elles ne vous enflamment pas et employer les baguettes à vos risques et périls.
Il est même possible de vous retrouver bloqué avec un équipement maudit, dans quel cas il faudra attendre un parchemin de délivrance pour pouvoir vous en débarrasser.

 [h1]La prudence est une vertu[/h1]

Les combats ne rapportent que rarement la moindre récompense et tendent à user des ressources, il est donc souvent intéressant de les éviter quand c'est possible. Pour cela, il est possible de jouer la carte de la discrétion en se glissant le long des murs sombres, ou de courir jusqu'à ce que l'ennemi se désintéresse de nous.
Le donjon est très peu linéaires et il existe bien des manières de le parcourir. Un monstre trop dangereux ou un boss trop difficile pourra donc être laissé de côté pour y revenir plus tard avec une meilleure préparation.
Les niveaux ont souvent plusieurs issues et il existe une grande variété d'environnements, tant en terme de décors que de difficultés. Certains sont remplis de hordes grouillantes de monstres qu'il faudra éviter discrètement, certains sont si sombres qu'il faudra avoir une large quantité de torches, d'autres sont remplis de pièges ou de dangers environnementaux qui mettrons à l'épreuve l'agilité et l'attention du joueur.

[h1]Un complexe souterrain[/h1]

Votre exploration ne sera pas qu'un enchaînement de combat et les couloirs du donjon abritent bien des secrets. Bien des choses peuvent mener un joueur à une découverte intéressante, un élément de décors d'apparence banale, quelques indices sonores ou la lecture d'un des nombreux morceaux de textes donnant des indices sur les mystères du donjon.
Des enclumes permettrons de combiner des objets entre eux pour les améliorés et de rares boutiques vous vendrons de quoi survivre un peu plus longtemps. Des puzzles environnementaux permettent de varier les plaisirs et nécessiterons bien souvent d'employer des informations trouvés ailleurs dans le donjon ou de manipuler tout un tas d'activateur pour avancer dans les niveaux les plus tortueux. Si ce genre de casse tête parfois lent vous ennuie, vous ne perdrez pas grand chose en les ignorants complètements et le nombre de puzzles peut même être réglé dans les options.
Certaines clés ou solutions ne pourrons être trouvées que plus tard dans le donjon, certains lieux ne pourrons être atteint qu'en descendant directement dans un trou, croisant peut-être les monstres tombés ici avant vous.

[h1]Le chaos engendre la beauté[/h1]

Si le système de combat peut paraître maladroit et peu pratique, il est au service d'une vision stratégique plus large où le moindre combat peut mener à la mort et la moindre ressource devient un atout déterminant.
La génération procédurale est la plus grande force du jeu, les donjons sont variés, riches, interconnectés et donnent réellement l'impression d'un tout plutôt qu'une simple succession de niveaux.
Une suite est prévue pour 2022, qui promet de reprendre les points forts du jeu et d'y apporter bien plus encore. A surveiller, donc !
